summary.text: Ohm's law links the current through a conductor to the voltage across it, with resistance as the constant that connects them.
It is an empirical rule that describes most conducting materials accurately over many orders of magnitude of current, though some non-ohmic materials do not obey it.
Paul Drude's 1900 model explained it: a voltage speeds electrons along, collisions with atoms turn their energy into heat, and the average drift grows with the field.

facts.label: Named after
facts.value: German physicist Georg Ohm, who published in 1827

facts.label: Conductance
facts.value: G equals 1 divided by the resistance R

facts.label: Earlier finding
facts.value: Henry Cavendish found voltage and current rise together in 1781, unpublished

facts.label: Electron model
facts.value: Paul Drude proposed it in 1900, the first classical one

items.prompt: A lamp's filament passes more current as the voltage rises, but its resistance changes a lot along the way. Does it follow Ohm's law?

options.label: Yes, because current always rises with voltage
Yes, because every material obeys the law
No, because resistance must stay constant
No, because a lamp is not a conductor

items.explain: Ohm's law says the resistance is constant, independent of current; if it varies, the relation is only a definition of static resistance.

items.prompt: In the Drude picture of a wire, electrons are pushed along by an electric field but keep bumping into atoms. Where does their lost motion energy go?

options.label: Into heat in the material
Into extra charge on the atoms
Into a stronger electric field
Into making the electrons heavier

items.explain: Collisions scatter the electrons and convert their kinetic energy into thermal energy.

items.prompt: When Ohm first published his results, many German critics attacked them. What was behind much of that hostility?

options.label: His measurements had been shown to be faulty
A view that truth comes from reasoning, not experiments
His results had already been published by Cavendish
A ban on research into electric currents

items.explain: The prevailing philosophy held that experiments were unnecessary because nature is well ordered and can be understood by reasoning alone.

items.prompt: Cavendish measured the link between voltage and current before Ohm, yet Ohm gets the credit. Why?

options.label: Cavendish had made errors, so his work was discarded
Cavendish only studied static electricity
Ohm's work was copied from Cavendish and renamed
Cavendish shared nothing, and his results surfaced in 1879

items.explain: He did not tell other scientists, and his results stayed unknown until James Clerk Maxwell published them in 1879.

items.prompt: In the electron model of a wire, why does doubling the voltage roughly double the current?

options.label: The average drift speed is proportional to the field
The wire gains twice as many free electrons
The electrons collide only half as often
The atoms in the wire stop moving

items.explain: The average drift velocity of electrons, and so the current, is proportional to the electric field and thus the voltage.

items.prompt: Ohm's law is called an empirical law. What does that mean?

options.label: It was derived from first principles with no tests
It applies to every material in every situation
It only holds for materials made of metal
It rests on measurements of real materials

items.explain: An empirical relation comes from measurement, and this one accurately describes most conductive materials over many orders of magnitude of current.
